title: Quota shepherding and regional fencing — architecture notes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a lightweight, operationalizable approach we can iterate on for tenant-aware routing across regions including quota enforcement, contract-aware prioritization, and noisy-neighbor containment. Aim is to produce a pragmatic control plane sketch and a set of runnable mitigations (throttles, fences, ejections) rather than a perfect formal model.

Context and motivation:
- Growth in multi-tenant usage means a few noisy customers can intermittently reduce tail latency for others.
- We need a mechanism that respects contracts (reserved throughput, SLAs), provides predictable isolation, and is cheap to operate in regional failure/fallback scenarios.
- Existing heuristics (simple rate limits, global eviction) are too coarse. We want "quota shepherding" — continuous, low-friction shaping that preserves SLA commitments.

Assumptions:
- Tenants have metadata: tier (free/prod/enterprise), reserved_units (tokens/sec or rps), contract_slo (p99 latency target, availability), regions_allowed (list).
- Serving runtime emits per-request traces: tenant_id, model_variant, tokens, start_ts, end_ts, node_id, region, queue_time, parse_time, compute_time.
- Control plane can push short-lived routing policies (< 30s TTL) and node-level enforcement knobs (token buckets, priority queues, eviction directives).

Key concepts / glossary (operational):
- Quota shepherding: continuously adjusting target ingress shares for tenants to prevent overconsumption while preserving reserved guarantees.
- Capacity fence: a soft isolation boundary per region, defined by reserved vs. best-effort pools. Fences can be tightened during contention to protect reserved capacity.
- SLA elasticity index (SEI): a score (0..1) per tenant indicating how elastic their SLA is for temporary degradation; derived from contract terms, support tier, and explicit customer flags.
- Tenant momentum score: short-window rate + recent error/latency trend used to detect spikes or runaway workloads.

High-level decision flow (per-region):
1) Ingest telemetry per-tenant (1s granularity): request rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, errored_count, queued_len, model_type mix.
2) Compute signals: momentum, SEI, reserve_utilization (reserved_rps_used / reserved_rps), best_effort_utilization.
3) Contention detection: if overall utilization > region_capacity_threshold (e.g., 85%) or p99 across top tenants rises > baseline, mark region under contention.
4) Apply policy matrix:
   - If tenant has reserved_units and reserve_utilization > 100% -> preferential throttle non-reserved bursts (move to best-effort queue or spill to other region if allowed).
   - If tenant is enterprise + SEI low (inelastic) -> honor reserved first, degrade best-effort tenants.
   - If tenant has runaway momentum (high derivative of rate) -> apply token-bucket shaping + background eviction to tail of requests (e.g., long-context or large-token requests).
   - If noisy-small-requests pattern (many tiny requests causing scheduling churn) -> coalesce requests server-side or apply minibatching windows per tenant.
5) If local mitigation insufficient -> trigger cross-region fallback (if tenant allowed) or reduced-quality fallback (serve quantized model variant).

Control plane components (minimal viable):
- Signal aggregator: short-window metrics collector (1s/5s rollups) per region/tenant.
- Policy engine: rule evaluator that outputs policy deltas (token bucket params, queue weights, region-preference hints).
- Enforcement API: lightweight push to nodes to update runtime knobs within 100–300ms.
- Orchestration agent (per region): manages region-wide fences and coordinates cross-region shifts.
- Audit log: append-only event stream for changes (who/why/trigger metrics).

Runtime enforcement primitives (what nodes need):
- Per-tenant token buckets with two counters: reserved_bucket and shared_bucket.
- Priority queue weights and preemption thresholds.
- Eviction hints: node-local flag to drop requests with specific predicates (e.g., model_variant=large && tokens>500 && tenant.elastic=true).
- Short-circuit routing hint: forward to another region or lower-cost model variant.

Noisy neighbor detection heuristics:
- High momentum ratio: (rate_15s / rate_5m) > spike_threshold (e.g., 4x).
- Latency amplification: tenant p99 increases faster than median across tenants in same tier.
- Resource skew: tenant consumes > X% of local active KV cache entries or GPU memory-worth-of-contexts.
- Error-density: elevated error-per-request combined with retry storms.
- Composite score > threshold triggers mitigation sequence.

Mitigation sequence (gradual, reversible):
1) Soft shape: reduce shared_bucket by 10–30% for offending tenant; add 200–500ms batching for small requests.
2) Promote reserved vs shared: if victim tenants exist, increase their weights temporarily using capacity fences.
3) Tiered shedding: drop/deny excess best-effort requests with informative retry-after headers.
4) Eviction to fallback: route heavy requests to quantized model variant or to a lower-SLA region (with customer consent or pre-negotiated fallback).
5) Contracted escalation: if mitigation persists > window (e.g., 5m) for an enterprise tenant, open a pager and apply a softer cap to avoid SLA breach while ops engages.

Multi-region playbook notes:
- Prefer hot-standby regions for enterprise tenants: maintain a small reserved shadow capacity so cross-region failover is low-latency.
- Respect data locality: only spill to other regions when allowed by tenant policy. Route hints must carry tenant_data_policy.
- Split-brain avoidance: use conservative TTLs on control-plane policies and prefer divergence in favour of tenant isolation if network partition occurs.
- Cross-region cost accounting: charge overage / fallback differently; surfaced in billing and Console so customers see effects.

Telemetry and SLOs for platform team (example):
- Decision latency: 95% of policy pushes applied within 400ms.
- Corrective efficiency: percent reduction in p99 for victims within 2 minutes of mitigation >= 60%.
- False positives: fraction of noisy-neighbor mitigations that were later rolled back because they affected non-offenders < 5%.
- Stability: mitigations should not oscillate more than N times per hour (tunable).

Operational UX and customer-facing signals:
- Console: show active tenant fences, current reserve utilization, and any active fallbacks with reasons.
- Alerts: tenants experiencing >10% of requests denied or >2% routed to fallback should generate CS notifications.
- Runbooks: quick guide for SREs to inspect tenant momentum, force-evict, or lift fences manually.

Open questions and risks:
- How to encode legally binding fallback rights in contracts? Need legal + sales input.
- Billing model complexity when cross-region fallback occurs frequently.
- Edge cases where many mid-tier tenants align and collectively look like a single noisy tenant; need fairness heuristics to avoid mass shedding.
- Risk of user-visible retries when we coalesce/shape — product needs to define acceptable UX degradation.

Next steps / action items (owner tags):
- Prototype policy engine rules in a simulator (Marco Ruiz) — create JIRA for scenarios + golden traces.
- Implement a minimal enforcement API on runtime (Sana Gupta) — feature flag gated.
- Draft contract fallback language with Legal & Sales (Aisha Patel) — due EOW.
- Build Console view for active fences and per-tenant metrics (Liam O'Connor) — design review in 2 weeks.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add example JSON policy schema (TTL, weights, bucket_sizes, spill_region) — simulate.
- Run archival queries to estimate how often tenants exceed reserved units historically (baseline).
- Add integration test to ensure policy push rollback semantics are safe when not acknowledged.

References / links:
- See related design brainstorming in CONFLUENCE-1234 (tenant routing heuristics)
- Simulator PR: github.com/redwood-inference/tenant-routing#45

End of note.
